title: Putana, and why Krishna comes
hookLine: a lovely stranger brings poison to Nanda's house, and the baby she came to kill ends her
carry: an avatar comes to protect the good
tomorrow: the sweet smoke of Putana's pyre

lines: SHE WALKS TO THE BABY'S BED.
cards: Nanda is away in Mathura, paying his dues to the king, and Vasudeva, meeting him there, has warned him: go home quickly, there may be trouble in Gokula. Back in the village, a woman arrives.
She is beautiful, the Bhagavata says, with flowers in her hair, a soft smile, a graceful walk. The cowherd women think a goddess has come to visit.
She walks straight into Nanda's house, to the bed where the baby is lying.

teach.h: A KILLER IN A LOVELY FORM
teach.b: Putana is one of Kamsa's killers. The Bhagavata calls her a demoness who goes from town to town killing infants, and today, by her magic, she has taken the form of a lovely woman.
And the people guarding the child, Yashoda and Rohini, are so struck by her sweetness that they just stand there and watch her lift him. The danger doesn't break in. It's welcomed.

Then the text turns the picture around: Putana takes the child on her lap the way someone picks up a sleeping snake, thinking it's a rope. As she comes near, the baby closes his eyes; the verse doesn't say why.
She offers him her breast, smeared with poison. He feeds, and draws her very life out with it.

She screams, let go, let go, and the earth shakes. As she dies, her disguise falls away, and her true body crashes down, crushing trees. On top of it, the cowherd women find the baby, playing, unafraid.
Why does a baby god begin his life fighting demons? Krishna answers that himself, years later, in the Bhagavad Gita.

teach.h: AVATAR: HE COMES TO PROTECT THE GOOD
teach.b: Whenever dharma, the right order of things, falls apart, I come, age after age, to protect the good and to end the work of the wicked. Hindus call this coming down an avatar.
Putana kills babies; the first thing the infant Krishna does is stop her. In Hindu teaching, that's what the Lord's coming is for: to stand with the ones who can't protect themselves.

how: The killing of Putana is told in the Bhagavata Purana's tenth book and is one of the childhood episodes Hindus retell in songs, dance-dramas and temple art; Hindus call each such coming of the Lord to earth an avatar.

o: a goddess who visits Gokula to bless the newborn
a nurse from Mathura hired to care for the baby
Kamsa's killer, who comes looking lovely, with poison

p: the Lord coming down to earth
to protect the good, age after age

s: Putana breaks into the house by force
she walks in smiling, and the women let her pick up the child.
the baby draws out Putana's life as he feeds
she cries "let go, let go" and dies in her true form.
in the Gita, Krishna says he comes to earth to win glory in battle
he says he comes age after age to protect the good and restore dharma.

games.q: Rohan asks why the Lord comes to earth at all. which line from the Gita fits Putana's story?
o: I come age after age to protect the good.
do your work without clinging to its fruit.
the self is never born and never dies.
games.why: Gita 4.8: he comes age after age to protect the good and end wrongdoing. Putana was killing infants, and the baby stopped her.

practice: Many Hindus keep one name of Krishna close for hard moments: Krishna, or Govinda, a name from his childhood among the cowherds.
Bring to mind one person who can't easily protect themselves: a small child, an elder, someone being picked on. Say the name quietly a few times, holding them in mind.
If you don't pray, hold them in steady good wishes, and notice one small way you could stand on their side this week.

wordCard.voice: Putana. A killer sent by Kamsa, who comes to the baby as a beautiful woman with poison, and whose life he draws out.

orig.note: putana: the name of the demoness sent by Kamsa to kill infants.
